title: Find All Possible Stable Binary Arrays I
statement:
A binary array (every element is `0` or `1`) is **stable** when all of these hold:

- it contains exactly `zero` elements equal to `0`,
- it contains exactly `one` elements equal to `1`, and
- every contiguous subarray whose length is greater than `limit` contains at least one `0` and at least one `1`.

Return how many different stable arrays exist. The count can be huge, so return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.
signature: int numberOfStableArrays(int zero, int one, int limit)
notes:
## Intuition

The third rule simply says that no run of equal values may be longer than `limit`. Listing all arrangements (a brute force) is exponential, but a stable array is described well enough by how many zeros and ones it has used and which value it ends with. That suggests a DP over `(zeros used, ones used, last value)`.

To build an array that ends in `0`, append a `0` to any shorter stable array. That is only wrong when the new `0` makes a run of `limit + 1` zeros; such arrays are exactly "an array ending in `1`, then `limit + 1` zeros", and we subtract them.

## Approach

1. `endZero[i][j]` counts stable arrays with `i` zeros and `j` ones that end in `0`; `endOne[i][j]` is the same for arrays that end in `1`.
2. Base cases: an array of only zeros is stable when it has at most `limit` of them, so `endZero[i][0] = 1` for `i <= limit`; likewise `endOne[0][j] = 1` for `j <= limit`.
3. For `i, j >= 1`: `zeros = endZero[i-1][j] + endOne[i-1][j]`, minus `endOne[i-limit-1][j]` when `i > limit`. Compute `ones` the same way with the roles swapped.
4. Store both modulo `10^9 + 7` (add `MOD` back so a subtraction never leaves a negative value).
5. The answer is `endZero[zero][one] + endOne[zero][one]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`zero = 1, one = 1, limit = 2`. The base cases give `endZero[1][0] = 1` (`[0]`) and `endOne[0][1] = 1` (`[1]`). For `i = 1, j = 1`: `zeros = endZero[0][1] + endOne[0][1] = 0 + 1 = 1` (that is `[1,0]`) and `ones = endZero[1][0] + endOne[1][0] = 1 + 0 = 1` (`[0,1]`). Neither index exceeds `limit`, so nothing is subtracted, and the answer is `1 + 1 = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(zero × one): each cell is filled in constant time.
- Space: O(zero × one) for the two tables.

## Pitfalls

- Subtract the over-long run instead of looping over every run length; the loop works here but costs an extra factor of `limit`.
- After subtracting, the value can be negative modulo `MOD`; normalise with `(x % MOD + MOD) % MOD`.
- Base cases stop at `limit`: `[0, 0, 0]` is not stable when `limit = 2`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `endZero[i][j]` | stable arrays with `i` zeros and `j` ones ending in `0` |
| `endOne[i][j]` | stable arrays with `i` zeros and `j` ones ending in `1` |
| `i`, `j` | zeros and ones used so far |
| `zeros`, `ones` | the new counts for `endZero[i][j]` and `endOne[i][j]` before reduction |

narration.3: endZero[i][j] counts stable arrays with i zeros and j ones whose last value is 0.
narration.4: endOne[i][j] counts the same arrays but ending in 1.
narration.5: An array of only zeros is stable while it has at most limit of them...
narration.6: ...so each such length contributes exactly one array.
narration.8: Arrays of only ones work the same way...
narration.9: ...one array for each length up to limit.
narration.11: Fill the tables for every count of zeros...
narration.12: ...and every count of ones, both at least 1.
narration.13: Append a 0 to any stable array with one fewer zero.
narration.14: If i exceeds limit, some of those arrays now end in limit + 1 zeros.
narration.15: Those are an array ending in 1 followed by limit + 1 zeros; remove them.
narration.17: Append a 1 to any stable array with one fewer one.
narration.18: If j exceeds limit, some of those arrays end in limit + 1 ones.
narration.19: Remove the arrays ending in 0 followed by limit + 1 ones.
narration.21: Reduce modulo MOD, adding MOD back in case the subtraction went negative.
narration.25: Stable arrays with all the zeros and ones end in either value; add both.
